newsitem.title: CHILE: Canada, Chile clinch free-trade agreement.
newsitem.headline: Canada, Chile clinch free-trade agreement.

text.p: Chile and Canada finished negotiating a free-trade agreement Thursday and their leaders will initial the deal in Ottawa on Monday, negotiators for both countries said.
The pact calls for tariffs covering 80 percent of trade between Chile and Canada to disappear as soon as it goes into effect, said Chilean Finance Minister Eduardo Aninat.

Most of the rest will be phased out over 15 years, including those on meats, most grains and other farm items, with a handful of sensitive items keeping their tariffs for 18 years, he told a news conference.
"We have concluded a long process of negotiation that will link Chile with one of the world's seven largest economies," Aninat said.

President Eduardo Frei and Canada's Prime Minister Jean Chretien will initial the accord on Monday, but the actual signing will have to wait until legal copies have been drawn up in Spanish, English and French.
Both countries' legislatures will also have to approve the pact before it can take effect, Chilean officials said.

The agreement adds to a series of free trade agreements that Chile, with Latin America's strongest economy, has signed with various trading partners. It signed a free-trade deal with other Latin American nations in June, and has signed trade agreements with the European Union and Mexico.

Apart from phasing out tariffs, the deal also sets rules for trade in a wide array of services ranging from banking to telecommunications. It also includes sections on protecting labour rights and the environment in line with rules in the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA), Aninat said.
"The agreement goes quite a long way beyond just tariffs," he said.
Officials on both sides said the agreement would ease Chile's way into NAFTA. But its entrance into the pact will depend on the U.S. Congress approving "fast track" authority for U.S. negotiators.

The announcements -- by Aninat in Santiago and Canada's International Trade Minister Art Eggleton in Ottawa -- followed a series of contradictory statements in both capitals all day about whether the deal was ready or not.

In a sign that some differences may still need to be ironed out, Canada's chief negotiator Keith Christie said Chile had agreed to allow Canadians to invest without requiring they deposit 30 percent of their investment in the Central Bank.
But Aninat said earlier there was no change in Chile's policy, which calls for some financial investments to be subjected to the reserve requirement. Both sides agreed loans are subject to the rule.
Aninat was not available for comment on Christie's statement. A spokesman said the minister would make an announcement on Friday.
